etymology: From the surname Elliott; a nineteenth-century English hymn-writer, author of Just As I Am.
biblical_def: Charlotte Elliott was a nineteenth-century English hymn-writer, long an invalid, who is best remembered for the hymn Just As I Am, Without One Plea. It was born of her own coming to Christ. When she was troubled in soul and asked the preacher Caesar Malan how she might come to God, he bade her come just as she was, a sinner with nothing of her own to bring; and out of that counsel grew the hymn that has drawn more souls to Christ than perhaps any other of its kind. The dictionary honours Elliott for setting to song the gospel of free grace, that the sinner comes to Christ not on the ground of any worth or work, but empty-handed, resting on the promise that him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out (Joh 6:37). Her hymn is the very voice of the invitation, Whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely (Rev 22:17), and of the LORD’s own word, Though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow (Isa 1:18). Out of long affliction and weakness she gave the church a hymn of pure dependence upon Christ, that teaches every sinner to lay aside his pleas and come just as he is to the Saviour who receives him.

corruption_paragraphs: What is honourable in Charlotte Elliott is the pure gospel of her great hymn. Against every notion that the sinner must first make himself fit to come to Christ, Just As I Am sets the truth that he comes empty-handed, with no plea but the blood of the Lamb, and is received. The dictionary honours this hymn of free grace, born of the author’s own coming to the Saviour.

Out of long affliction Elliott gave the church a hymn of pure dependence upon Christ, teaching every burdened soul to lay aside its pleas and come to the Saviour who turns none away.

etymology: From the surname Medley; an eighteenth-century Particular Baptist minister and hymn-writer, once a sailor.
biblical_def: Samuel Medley was an eighteenth-century Particular Baptist minister and hymn-writer who had once been a sailor in the king’s navy, wounded in battle and brought to Christ through the reading of a sermon during his recovery. He became a faithful pastor at Liverpool and the author of many hymns of warm and personal devotion, chief among them I Know That My Redeemer Lives and O Could I Speak the Matchless Worth. His hymns dwell upon the living and reigning Christ, taking up the ancient confession of Job, I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth (Job 19:25). The dictionary honours Medley as a singer of the living Redeemer, who rejoiced that now is Christ risen from the dead, and become the firstfruits of them that slept (1Co 15:20), and who rested on the truth that Christ ever liveth to make intercession, and is able to save to the uttermost them that come unto God by Him (Heb 7:25). His hymns press home the comfort that no charge can stand against the people of a Redeemer who died, and rose, and lives at God’s right hand to plead for them (Rom 8:34). Out of a sailor’s rough beginning, grace made a hymn-writer whose songs of the living Christ still gladden the church.

etymology: From the surname Kent; a Particular Baptist hymn-writer of Devon, a shipwright by trade, singer of sovereign grace.
biblical_def: John Kent was a Particular Baptist hymn-writer of Devon, a working shipwright with little schooling, who became one of the sweetest singers of free and sovereign grace among the English Baptists. His hymns, gathered as Kent’s Hymns and treasured among the Particular Baptists, dwell with delight upon the eternal love of God, the everlasting covenant, and the security of the elect in Christ. He sang that where sin abounded, grace did much more abound (Rom 5:20), and that the saints are made accepted in the beloved, to the praise of the glory of God’s grace (Eph 1:6). The dictionary honours Kent as a hymn-writer of sovereign grace, who rested all his hope on the truth that God hath saved us and called us with an holy calling, not according to our works, but according to His own purpose and grace, given us in Christ before the world began (2Ti 1:9). His hymns answer the trembling conscience with the challenge of the apostle, Who shall lay any thing to the charge of God’s elect? It is God that justifieth (Rom 8:33). From the shipyard came a poet of grace whose verses, plain and unpolished as they are, carry the deep comfort of the doctrines of grace into the hearts of the simple, and teach them to glory not in themselves but in the free favour of God.

etymology: From the surname Beddome; an eighteenth-century Baptist pastor of Bourton-on-the-Water and prolific hymn-writer.
biblical_def: Benjamin Beddome was an eighteenth-century Baptist pastor who laboured for over half a century in the one village church of Bourton-on-the-Water in the Cotswolds. He had the rare custom of composing a hymn for each of his sermons, that his people might sing the truth he had just preached, and in this way he wrote some eight hundred hymns, plain and pointed and full of Scripture, among them the well-loved Did Christ o’er Sinners Weep. His hymnody is a model of the union of preaching and praise, the word of Christ dwelling richly in the people as they taught and admonished one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs (Col 3:16). The dictionary honours Beddome as a faithful pastor whose hymns served his preaching, setting the doctrine of the sermon upon the lips and in the hearts of his flock. He sang of the Saviour who beheld the city and wept over it (Luk 19:41), and taught his people that he that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him (Psa 126:6). His long and quiet ministry in one place, and his hymns wedded to his sermons, teach that the singing of the church is to be the echo of her preaching, and that praise and doctrine are best when they go hand in hand.

etymology: From the surname Haweis; an eighteenth-century evangelical Anglican, hymn-writer and a founder of the missionary movement.
biblical_def: Thomas Haweis was an eighteenth-century evangelical clergyman of the Church of England, a physician turned minister, a hymn-writer, and one of the chief founders and promoters of the modern missionary movement. He was a friend of the leaders of the Evangelical Revival and a tireless advocate for the carrying of the gospel to the heathen, and he had a great hand in the founding of the London Missionary Society and the sending of its first missionaries to the South Seas. His hymns, among them O Thou From Whom All Goodness Flows, breathe a warm evangelical devotion. The dictionary honours Haweis as a hymn-writer and a missionary statesman whose heart was set upon the prayer of the psalm, That thy way may be known upon earth, thy saving health among all nations (Psa 67:2). He laboured that the gospel might be preached to every creature (Mar 16:15), knowing that men cannot believe in Him of whom they have not heard, and that they cannot preach except they be sent, and how beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace (Rom 10:15). His union of hymnody and missionary zeal teaches that the praise of the church and the spread of the gospel belong together, and that the people who sing the goodness of God will long to make His way known among all nations.

etymology: From the surname Ryland; an eighteenth-century Particular Baptist minister, hymn-writer, and supporter of the missionary movement.
biblical_def: John Ryland was an eighteenth-century Particular Baptist minister, president of the Bristol Baptist Academy, a hymn-writer, and one of the small band who, with William Carey and Andrew Fuller, launched the modern missionary movement among the Baptists. He is remembered for the hymn Sovereign Ruler of the Skies, a serene confession of the all-governing providence of God, and for his part in the founding of the Baptist Missionary Society. His hymns rest upon the great truth that the LORD hath prepared His throne in the heavens, and His kingdom ruleth over all (Psa 103:19). The dictionary honours Ryland as a singer of the sovereignty of God and a friend of missions, who believed that God doeth according to His will in the army of heaven and among the inhabitants of the earth, and none can stay His hand (Dan 4:35). He rested in the truth that our God is in the heavens, and hath done whatsoever He hath pleased (Psa 115:3), and that all things work together for good to them that love God (Rom 8:28). His union of a humble trust in providence with a bold zeal for missions teaches that the doctrine of God’s sovereignty is no enemy to the spread of the gospel but its very ground; for the King whose kingdom ruleth over all will surely gather His own from every nation.

etymology: From the surname Palmer; a nineteenth-century American Congregationalist minister and hymn-writer.
biblical_def: Ray Palmer was a nineteenth-century American Congregationalist minister and hymn-writer, remembered above all for the hymn My Faith Looks Up to Thee, written as a young man in a season of loneliness and trial. He wrote it for himself, not for the church, and could never read it afterward without tears; yet it became one of the most beloved hymns of personal faith in the English tongue. The dictionary honours Palmer for setting to song the life of faith that looks away from self to Christ, after the pattern of the apostle, who bids us look unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith, who endured the cross and is set down at the right hand of God (Heb 12:2). His hymn is the very voice of the believer who says, I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me; and the life which I now live in the flesh I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me, and gave Himself for me (Gal 2:20). It is the song of those who, having not seen Christ, yet love Him, and believing, rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory (1Pe 1:8). Out of a young man’s trial came a hymn that has taught the whole church to lift its eyes from self to the Saviour.

etymology: From the surname Prentiss; a nineteenth-century American author and hymn-writer, author of More Love to Thee, O Christ.
biblical_def: Elizabeth Prentiss was a nineteenth-century American author and hymn-writer, the wife of a Presbyterian minister, who knew much of affliction, including the loss of children, and out of her sorrows learned to love Christ the more. She is remembered for the hymn More Love to Thee, O Christ, written in a time of grief, the prayer of a heart that asks for nothing of this world but a deeper love to its Saviour. The dictionary honours Prentiss for setting to song the chief commandment and the chief desire of the sanctified soul, to love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind, and with all thy strength (Mar 12:30). Her hymn is the cry of one who, in the trial of her faith, more precious than gold that perisheth though it be tried with fire (1Pe 1:7), counted all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus her Lord (Php 3:8). She had learned that nothing can separate the believer from the love of Christ, neither tribulation, nor distress, nor sword (Rom 8:35), and that affliction, sanctified, does not quench but deepens the soul’s love to its Saviour. Her hymn teaches the church to ask, in joy or grief, for more love to Christ above every earthly good.

etymology: From the surname Francis; a nineteenth-century English hymn-writer, author of O the Deep, Deep Love of Jesus.
biblical_def: Samuel Trevor Francis was a nineteenth-century English layman, a London merchant and a worker among the poor and the lost, who is remembered for the hymn O the Deep, Deep Love of Jesus. It was written, he tells, in a dark hour when he was tempted to despair, and the love of Christ was set before his soul as a boundless ocean in which he might rest. The dictionary honours Francis for giving the church a hymn that sounds the immeasurable love of Christ, after the prayer of the apostle that the saints might be able to comprehend with all saints what is the breadth, and length, and depth, and height, and to know the love of Christ, which passeth knowledge (Eph 3:18; Eph 3:19). His hymn dwells upon the love that the Lord Himself called the greatest, for greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends (Joh 15:13), the love that is not our love to God but His to us, herein is love, not that we loved God, but that He loved us, and sent His Son to be the propitiation for our sins (1Jo 4:10). His hymn teaches the troubled and the tempted to rest, as he rested, upon the deep, deep love of Jesus, a love vast as the ocean and free as the wide air, that bears the believer up when all else fails.

corruption_paragraphs: What is honourable in Samuel Trevor Francis is the great theme of his hymn, the boundless love of Christ. Tempted to despair, he was given to see that love as an ocean in which his soul might rest, and out of that hour came a hymn that has comforted countless saints. The dictionary honours this hymnody of the love of Christ that passeth knowledge.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is the immeasurable love of Christ, the love the apostle prayed the saints might comprehend in its breadth and length and depth and height. It is not our love to God but His to us, the greatest love, that lays down its life for its friends; herein is love, that He loved us and sent His Son to be the propitiation for our sins. Francis teaches the troubled and the tempted to rest upon this deep, deep love of Jesus, vast as the ocean, that bears the believer up when all else fails.

etymology: From the surname Hammond; an eighteenth-century hymn-writer of the evangelical revival, author of Awake, and Sing the Song.
biblical_def: William Hammond was an eighteenth-century hymn-writer of the evangelical revival, a Cambridge scholar who cast in his lot with the awakened people of God and laboured among the Calvinistic Methodists and the Moravian Brethren. He is remembered for the hymn Awake, and Sing the Song of Moses and the Lamb, a summons to the redeemed to praise their Saviour. The dictionary honours Hammond as a singer of the praise of the Lamb, who called the church to obey the psalmist’s charge, O sing unto the LORD a new song: sing unto the LORD, all the earth (Psa 96:1). His hymns echo the song of the redeemed in heaven, who sing a new song, saying, Thou art worthy to take the book, for thou wast slain, and hast redeemed us to God by thy blood out of every kindred, and tongue, and people, and nation (Rev 5:9). He bade the saints, O come, let us sing unto the LORD; let us make a joyful noise to the rock of our salvation (Psa 95:1), and speak to themselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in their heart to the Lord (Eph 5:19). His hymnody teaches that the proper answer of the redeemed to redeeming love is praise, and that the song of the church on earth is the rehearsal of the song of the Lamb that shall fill heaven for ever.

corruption_paragraphs: What is honourable in Hammond is his summons to the redeemed to praise their Saviour. His hymns call the church to sing a new song unto the LORD and to echo the song of the Lamb. The dictionary honours this hymnody of praise, which makes the answer of the saints to redeeming love a song.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is that the proper answer of the redeemed to redeeming love is praise. The psalmist bids us sing a new song, and make a joyful noise to the rock of our salvation; the redeemed in heaven sing the new song of the Lamb who was slain and redeemed them by His blood. Hammond teaches that the song of the church on earth is the rehearsal of the song that shall fill heaven for ever, and that a people bought with such a price cannot be silent, but must speak to themselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, making melody in their hearts to the Lord.
